$comment: The only source of a statistic in this knowledge base. Nothing numeric goes into prose unless it is here. Each entry carries its verdict: 'verified' (vendor documentation or a study with disclosed sample and method), 'directional' (real data, self-selected sample or vendor incentive, use for direction not magnitude), or 'folklore' (no primary source located). A folklore entry may only appear inside references/evidence-and-myths.md or an explicit debunking. See .kb/STYLE.md sections 1 and 7.

facts.claim: Share of the Fortune 500 running a detectable ATS
facts.sample: 489 of 500 companies
facts.method: career-page URL detection, data collected 2 June 2025, no company contacted
facts.source: Jobscan 2025 ATS Usage Report
facts.note: True and nearly content-free. 'Uses an ATS' means 'has an applicant database', the way 'uses email' means 'has a mail server'. It says nothing about automated rejection. Its rhetorical power in resume-service marketing comes entirely from the unstated leap to 'therefore a robot judges you'. Historical series: 98.2% (2018), 98.8% (2019), 97.4% (2023), 98.4% (2024). Jobscan's own homepage rounds this to 99%, which is a vendor inflating its own research.

facts.claim: Workday Recruiting share of Fortune 500 career pages
facts.sample: 489 detected of the Fortune 500
facts.source: Jobscan 2025 ATS Usage Report

facts.claim: SAP SuccessFactors share of Fortune 500 career pages
facts.source: Jobscan 2025 ATS Usage Report

facts.claim: ATS share across a broad company sample
facts.value: Greenhouse 19.3%, Lever 16.6%, Workday 15.9%, iCIMS 15.3%
facts.sample: 12,820 companies
facts.source: Jobscan 2025 ATS Usage Report

facts.claim: ATS share among top-rated employers, company-weighted
facts.value: Greenhouse 49.0%, Workday 21.8%, Lever 8.0%, Ashby 7.0%, Oracle HCM 2.8%, iCIMS 0.7%
facts.sample: 3,223 employers
facts.method: career-page crawl detecting the ATS serving the application flow, each employer counted once regardless of size
facts.source: ResumeGeni ATS Market Share 2026
facts.note: Sampling artefact, not a contradiction of the Jobscan numbers. 'Top-rated employers' skews to US tech and VC-backed companies, which is Greenhouse/Lever/Ashby territory. iCIMS at 0.7% here versus 10.7% of revenue reflects that retail, healthcare, manufacturing, logistics, banking and the public sector are under-represented. Which ATS a candidate faces is a function of sector and company size, not a global ranking.

facts.claim: Global ATS software market by revenue, and the leading vendor
facts.value: $2.5B, growing 12.3% year over year; iCIMS leads at 10.7%; top 10 vendors together are 51.1%
facts.source: Apps Run The World, ATS market segment
facts.note: The long tail is nearly half the market. 2024 data, ageing.

facts.claim: Share of CV documents using a column layout
facts.value: at least 15%
facts.source: Textkernel engineering blog, Improving extraction from column resumes

facts.claim: Textkernel gap-classification accuracy after replacing a rule-based classifier with gradient boosting
facts.value: 82% to 91% overall; 60% to 82% on the gaps that are genuinely column separators
facts.sample: subjective well-rendered rate measured on ~700 documents; contact-field fill rates on 12,000+ CVs
facts.source: Textkernel engineering blog, Improving extraction from column resumes
facts.note: The single most important number for the column question. After a dedicated ML investment by the market-leading parser vendor, 18% of true column separators are still misclassified — and Textkernel is the good case, a specialist. It also still emits fatal quality code 433 when it detects columns.

facts.claim: Textkernel subjective well-rendered CV rate, before and after the column-detection model
facts.sample: ~700 documents
facts.source: Textkernel engineering blog, Improving extraction from column resumes

facts.claim: Extraction F1 for naive OCR plus direct LLM versus a layout-aware pipeline
facts.value: 0.927 to 0.946 on synthetic and 0.919 to 0.959 on real resumes; on the complex long-form subgroup, 0.548 to 0.854
facts.sample: SynthResume 2,994 resumes; RealResume 13,100 real resumes from Alibaba's HR system
facts.source: Zhu et al., Layout-Aware Parsing Meets Efficient LLMs, arXiv 2510.09722
facts.note: The empirical core of the layout argument. On a typical resume a modern LLM parser loses only two to four points to layout; on complex or long-form content, naive extraction collapses to F1 0.548 and loses roughly half the information. Same paper: approximately 20% of resumes use non-linear multi-column layouts that break top-to-bottom left-to-right reading flow.

facts.claim: Textkernel coverage and throughput
facts.value: used by more than 60% of the HR technology industry; 2 billion documents processed annually; approximately 0.5 seconds per document; 29 languages for CV parsing including Italian
facts.source: Textkernel Extract product documentation
facts.note: The coverage figure is vendor marketing. The throughput and language figures are product specification.

facts.claim: Daxtra parser throughput, coverage and taxonomy
facts.value: more than 1 million documents per day; approximately 2 seconds for a two-page Word document; approximately 46 languages with full Italian support; 57 industries and 16,000+ skills expanding to approximately 100,000 aliases
facts.source: Daxtra Parser CVX Technical Specifications

facts.claim: Affinda parser performance and coverage
facts.value: median parse time 50 milliseconds; approximately 50 resumes per second per container; 100+ fields; 50+ languages
facts.source: Affinda Resume Parser

facts.claim: RChilli extraction coverage for Oracle HCM
facts.value: 140+ extracted fields, auto-populating approximately 27 to 30 Oracle HCM standard candidate fields
facts.source: RChilli for Oracle users

facts.claim: Workday questionnaire structure and eligibility mapping
facts.value: maximum 50 questions per questionnaire excluding branching, up to 6 levels of branching, and 12 mapped eligibility questions available for disqualification
facts.source: Workday Recruiting for Administrators, Job Requisition Components
facts.note: The 12 mapped eligibility questions cover age eligibility, legal work authorisation, sponsorship requirement, willingness to relocate, previous employment with the company, salary expectations, availability and notice period. Answers generate calculated fields usable in Automatic Stage Routing condition rules, and can carry positive or negative scores.

facts.claim: What Greenhouse auto-reject rules can act on
facts.value: custom job-post questions of type Yes/No, single-select or multi-select only, with AND across up to 5 questions and OR within a single question's options
facts.source: Greenhouse Support, Auto-reject and Application rules overview
facts.note: Cannot trigger on the resume, on free text, or on a match score. On auto-reject, recruiters subscribed to new-application notifications are not notified — no human sees it by default.

facts.claim: Greenhouse Job Board API submission requirements
facts.value: required fields are first_name, last_name and email, each under 255 characters; accepted resume file types are PDF, DOC, DOCX, TXT and RTF
facts.source: Greenhouse Job Board API developer documentation

facts.claim: Greenhouse maximum upload size for candidate documents
facts.value: 100 MB
facts.source: Greenhouse Support, supported formats
facts.note: The accepted ceiling is far above the size at which parsing stays reliable. Keep resumes well under 1 MB.

facts.claim: Oracle Taleo Connect Client extraction limits
facts.value: 500,000 records per day and 100,000 per extraction transaction
facts.source: Oracle Taleo to Oracle Recruiting migration documentation

facts.claim: What recruiters filter on inside the ATS
facts.value: skills 76.4%, educational background 59.7%, job titles 55.3%, certifications or licences 50.6%, years of experience 44.0%, location 43.4%; more than 99.7% use filters at all
facts.sample: 384 HR professionals directly involved in hiring
facts.method: random sampling via Zoho Surveys, February to March 2025
facts.source: Jobscan, State of the Job Search 2025
facts.note: The most actionable dataset in the field. Every one of these is a structured field the parser must have successfully extracted — which is why parsing matters, not because of a rejection bot but because a failed parse means absence from the query result set.

facts.claim: Recruiter sourcing channels and LinkedIn evaluation
facts.value: 75% source on LinkedIn, ahead of employee referrals at 60%, agencies 60%, social 55%, job boards 48% and their own ATS archive 41%; 73.3% always or often evaluate a candidate's LinkedIn profile
facts.sample: 384 HR professionals
facts.source: Jobscan, State of the Job Search 2025

facts.claim: Recruiters reporting their ATS does not auto-reject on formatting, content or design
facts.value: 92%, that is 23 of 25
facts.sample: 25 structured interviews with US recruiters across 10+ ATS platforms, companies from 120 to 50,000+ employees
facts.method: qualitative interviews, September to October 2025; authors state a 90% confidence interval of 2 to 21% for auto-rejection
facts.source: Enhancv, Does the ATS Reject Your Resume?
facts.note: Cite this carefully. It is 25 interviews, not a survey of thousands, and presenting it as a hard statistic repeats the sin of the 75% figure. In the same sample: 100% use knockout questions, 44% have AI match scores available and only 8% use them as hard rejection criteria.

facts.claim: Time recruiters actually spend on a resume
facts.value: 17 seconds for a short one-page resume, 27 seconds mid-length, 46 seconds long; fastest observed 12 seconds, slowest 2 minutes 27 seconds
facts.sample: 114 experienced recruiters, each shown a job description then three resumes of different lengths
facts.method: timed covertly via Microsoft Clarity; participants did not know they were being timed; resumes presented as images to prevent text search
facts.source: Jan Tegze, 2023
facts.note: Supersedes the six-second figure. The covert timing is what makes it stronger: it removes the demand characteristic that shaped the TheLadders result. Same author's survey work: over 70% of recruiters say they almost always or often skim, and 78% rate skimmability as highly important.

facts.claim: Recruiter preference for a two-page over a one-page resume
facts.value: 2.3 times more likely to select the two-page version overall; 1.4x at entry level, 2.6x mid-level, 2.9x managerial; quality rated 8.6 versus 7.1
facts.sample: 482 recruiters, hiring managers, HR professionals and C-suite; 7,712 resume selections recorded
facts.method: paired hiring simulation, 15 October to 2 November 2018; each one-page resume had a two-page counterpart for an equivalent candidate
facts.source: ResumeGo, Settling the Debate: One or Two Page Resumes
facts.note: The strongest evidence on length, and still weak: vendor-run, a simulation rather than a field experiment, and eight years old. A two-page resume also carries more information by construction, so this may partly measure content volume rather than page count. The seniority gradient is the durable finding.

facts.claim: Callback rate by cover letter type
facts.value: 10.7% with no cover letter, 12.5% generic, 16.4% tailored — a 53% lift for tailored over none
facts.sample: 7,287 applications to real job openings on ZipRecruiter, Glassdoor and Indeed
facts.method: field experiment with three arms, 15 July 2019 to 10 January 2020, callbacks tracked over 30 days
facts.source: ResumeGo, Cover Letters: Just How Important Are They?
facts.note: The only randomised field experiment on cover letters located. Vendor-run, unreplicated, per-arm sample sizes not published, and it involved submitting fictitious applications to real employers. It predates both the AI application flood and AI cover-letter generation, so the generic arm's value in 2026 is plausibly zero or negative. The direction — tailored beats generic beats none — is credible; treat the magnitude as an upper bound.

facts.claim: Initial screen passthrough for referred versus all candidates
facts.value: 52% versus 35%
facts.sample: 54M+ applications across 93,000 jobs, January 2021 to March 2026
facts.source: Ashby 2026 Talent Trends Report
facts.note: Same dataset: same-function referrals interview at 37% versus 26% cross-function, so who refers you matters. Offer acceptance for referrals runs 89% business and 84% technical.

facts.claim: Referred workers' quit rate relative to non-referred
facts.value: 10 to 30% less likely to quit; referred applicants are more likely to be hired and to accept offers despite similar observable skill characteristics
facts.sample: personnel data from nine large firms across call centres, trucking and high-tech
facts.source: Burks, Cowgill, Hoffman and Housman, The Value of Hiring through Employee Referrals, Quarterly Journal of Economics 130(2)
facts.note: The strongest positive finding in this entire literature, and the only peer-reviewed one. The advantage is not explained by referred candidates being better on paper — which is what makes it causal-ish rather than selection.

facts.claim: Applications per hire and interview probability
facts.value: tripled since 2021 to more than 300 per hire; candidates are approximately 50% less likely to receive an interview than five years ago; global median application-to-interview rate 3.6 to 4.7%
facts.sample: 100M+ applications across 200,000+ jobs, 2021 to 2026
facts.source: Ashby 2026 Talent Trends Report
facts.note: Skews toward tech, startup and scale-up employers. Offer conversion has surpassed 2021 levels — the funnel narrowed at the top, not the bottom.

facts.claim: Applications per job, per recruiter, and time to fill
facts.value: applications per job 116 to 244 between 2022 and 2025, up 111%; applications per recruiter per year 146 to 746, up 412%; recruiters per organisation 10.43 to 4.62, down 56%; time to fill 43.6 to 59.7 days
facts.sample: 6,000+ companies, 640M+ applications, 2022 to 2025
facts.source: Greenhouse, The Hire Standard Benchmark Report
facts.note: This is the real 2026 story. Human overload, not software rejection, is what filters most resumes.

facts.claim: Employers agreeing that qualified candidates are vetted out by over-narrow job criteria
facts.value: 88% for high-skills candidates, 94% for middle-skills
facts.sample: approximately 8,000 workers and 2,250 executives across the US, UK and Germany
facts.source: Fuller and Raman, Hidden Workers: Untapped Talent, Harvard Business School and Accenture
facts.note: This is the real study behind the mangled '88% of applications are auto-rejected' claim. It measures executives' self-assessment of their own over-specified job descriptions, not any rejection rate. The number survived the retelling and the meaning did not. Five years old and predates LLM screening entirely.

facts.claim: Resumes containing white text or hidden prompt injections, as measured rather than surveyed
facts.value: approximately 1% at Greenhouse in H1 2025; approximately 10% of AI-scanned resumes at ManpowerGroup, roughly 100,000 per year
facts.source: Greenhouse platform telemetry and ManpowerGroup statement to the New York Times

facts.claim: Job seekers admitting to hidden text or prompt injection, versus recruiters catching it
facts.value: 41% of US job seekers admit to it and 52% of the rest are considering it; 22% of recruiters report catching hidden prompt injections; 91% report spotting candidate deception of some kind
facts.sample: 4,136 respondents across the US, UK, Ireland and Germany, including 1,200 US job seekers and 665 US recruiters and hiring managers
facts.source: Greenhouse 2025 AI in Hiring Report
facts.note: Greenhouse sells detection tooling. Never cite the 41% alone: their own platform telemetry shows approximately 1%. The 40-fold gap between claimed and observed behaviour is the more interesting finding, and it means self-reported adoption of resume tricks is wildly inflated.

facts.claim: Hidden prompt injections in real resumes, and their growth
facts.value: approximately 1% of resumes contain hidden prompt injections, a sevenfold increase between July 2024 and November 2025; more than 90% of injected prompts do not use explicit instructions
facts.sample: approximately 200,000 real resumes, July 2019 to December 2025, from hireEZ
facts.method: de-identified corpus analysis with tailored high-precision detectors
facts.source: Zhang et al., Measuring Real-World Prompt Injection Attacks in LLM-based Resume Screening, USENIX Security Symposium 2026, arXiv 2605.28999
facts.note: The naive 'ignore all previous instructions' template is already the minority; most injections are disguised self-promotional text. The authors deliberately did not test whether injections changed hiring outcomes, on ethical grounds.

facts.claim: Conditions under which resume prompt injection works
facts.value: effective only when candidate quality is homogeneous and few candidates inject; effectiveness rapidly diminishes as more candidates inject and collapses when manipulation becomes widespread
facts.source: Baxi, Xu, Jiang and Jasin, Prompt Injection in Automated Resume Screening with LLMs, arXiv 2606.27287
facts.note: A strictly self-defeating arms race. The equilibrium payoff at current claimed adoption is approximately zero.

facts.claim: Automated and fraudulent application volume
facts.value: 22% of active job seekers admit using bots to apply automatically, rising to 31% among Gen Z; Gartner projects that by 2028, 25% of job applicants will be fake
facts.source: Greenhouse 2025 workforce research, citing Gartner

facts.claim: Field extraction rate by file format and by builder
facts.value: Google Docs 95% DOC versus 96% PDF; MS Office 88% DOC versus 85% PDF; template range within MS Office 36% to 100%
facts.sample: 47 templates across Google Docs, Enhancv, Canva and MS Office, tested against Indeed's ATS
facts.method: scoring extraction of name, phone, location, LinkedIn, summary, skills, education and experience
facts.source: Enhancv, Busting ATS Myths
facts.note: Enhancv scores its own product highest, so discount the builder ranking. The finding that matters is structural: the format effect is at most three points and runs in opposite directions, while the template effect spans 64 points. Format is not the dominant variable; the template is.

facts.claim: Field extraction rate for single-column versus two-column layouts
facts.value: 93% versus 86% overall; skills 65% versus 46%; LinkedIn 100% versus 82%; education approximately 100% versus 88%
facts.source: Enhancv, The State of Resume Parsing
facts.note: A modest overall gap that hides a severe section-level one: the skills block is where two-column layouts actually fail.

facts.claim: InMail lift from the public #OpenToWork photo frame
facts.value: on average 40% more InMails from recruiters
facts.sample: 3M+ members who used the frame
facts.source: LinkedIn official blog
facts.note: LinkedIn's own measurement on its own platform, which is the best possible source for this claim and also six years old.

facts.claim: Callback effect of including a photograph, by gender
facts.value: attractive men received nearly double the callbacks of plain-looking men and significantly more than no-photo; women with no picture had a significantly higher callback rate than either attractive or plain-looking women
facts.sample: 5,312 CVs sent in pairs to 2,656 real job openings in Israel
facts.method: paired field experiment; each pair was one CV without a picture and one with an attractive or plain-looking photo
facts.source: Ruffle and Shtudiner, Are Good-Looking People More Employable?, Management Science 61(8)
facts.note: One of the few places where the academic literature gives genuinely actionable gender-specific guidance. The authors propose same-sex screener effects as the mechanism: 24 of the 25 people screening CVs in their follow-up were women. Corroborated by field experiments in Italy (Economia Politica 2020) and Spain (IZA DP 16119).

facts.claim: EU AI Act high-risk obligations for recruitment AI
facts.value: Annex III standalone high-risk obligations deferred from 2 August 2026 to 2 December 2027; Annex I embedded systems to 2 August 2028; Article 50 transparency and Article 4 AI literacy duties unchanged and in force from 2 August 2026
facts.source: Regulation (EU) 2026/1744, the Digital Omnibus on AI, published in the Official Journal 24 July 2026 and in force 27 July 2026
facts.note: Recruitment, CV screening, candidate ranking, promotion and termination are Annex III high-risk. Political agreement 7 May 2026, European Parliament endorsement 16 June 2026 (423 for, 57 against, 174 abstentions), Council approval 29 June 2026. Sources published before July 2026 state the original 2 August 2026 date and are now wrong. Obligations are postponed, not removed.

facts.claim: EU AI Act maximum penalties
facts.value: up to 15,000,000 euro or 3% of global annual turnover, whichever is higher
facts.source: EU AI Act

facts.claim: Italian national AI law covering employment
facts.value: Law No. 132 of 23 September 2025, in force 10 October 2025; implementing decrees prohibit fully automated decision-making for recruitment, dismissal and disciplinary action
facts.source: Norton Rose Fulbright and K&L Gates analyses of Italian Law 132/2025
facts.note: Italy was the first EU member state to enact a national AI law. It creates a double layer of obligations alongside GDPR Article 22, independent of the AI Act deferral: an employer processing an Italian applicant that fully auto-rejects on an AI score is exposed under both.

facts.claim: GDPR Article 22 and the strictness of the 'solely automated' test
facts.value: a rubber-stamp human review does not break the chain; if the human has no real ability or authority to override the output, the decision remains solely automated
facts.source: CJEU SCHUFA ruling C-634/21, December 2023
facts.note: Binding since May 2018 and therefore the sharper instrument today, given the AI Act deferral. In September 2025 the Hamburg data protection authority fined a financial services provider approximately 500,000 euro under Articles 22 and 13 to 15 for automated assessment without adequately explaining the logic of rejections.

facts.claim: NYC Local Law 144 requirements and penalties
facts.value: annual independent bias audit with published adverse-impact results, plus candidate notice at least 10 business days before use; penalties 500 to 1,500 dollars per violation
facts.source: NYC Department of Consumer and Worker Protection, and the New York State Comptroller audit of enforcement
facts.note: A December 2025 State Comptroller audit found enforcement had been minimal and complaint-driven, and recommended a proactive posture. Expect stricter enforcement.

facts.claim: EU Pay Transparency Directive obligations affecting application forms
facts.value: transposition deadline 7 June 2026; employers must disclose initial pay level or range in the posting or before the interview, and may not ask candidates about current or past pay
facts.source: Jackson Lewis, Understanding the EU Pay Transparency Directive
facts.note: Removes 'what is your current salary' from EU application forms. 'What are your salary expectations' remains legal and remains a live knockout field.

facts.claim: Vendor liability for ATS screening under US employment law
facts.value: Workday can be liable as an agent of employers because it performs screening functions employers would otherwise do themselves; nationwide ADEA collective action conditionally certified 16 May 2025, California FEHA claims survived dismissal June 2026
facts.source: Mobley v. Workday, N.D. Cal.
facts.note: The best explanation for why every ATS vendor's 2026 documentation aggressively disclaims auto-rejection and emphasises human-in-the-loop. It is legal risk management, and it shrinks the auto-reject surface in the candidate's favour.

facts.claim: 75% of resumes are rejected by an ATS before a human sees them
facts.value: no study, no dataset, no method ever published
facts.source: traced to Preptel, a resume-optimisation vendor promoting the figure around 2012; the company ceased operations in August 2013
facts.note: The figure circulates as 70%, 75% and 88% with no anchor, which is the diagnostic sign of a fabricated statistic: a real one has a single value and a single method. It was laundered through an uncited trade-press mention and now appears on university career pages.

facts.claim: 40% of applications are auto-rejected by machines before a human sees them
facts.value: origin not locatable in any study, vendor dataset or survey
facts.source: appears only as a bare assertion in aggregator posts
facts.note: The nearest real statistic is the Harvard Business School finding recorded under hbs-hidden-workers, which says something materially different.

facts.claim: Recruiters look at a resume for six seconds
facts.value: 6 seconds in 2012, restated as 7.4 seconds in 2018
facts.sample: approximately 30 recruiters
facts.method: eye-tracking, participants instructed toward speed; selection method undisclosed, never peer-reviewed, never replicated
facts.source: TheLadders
facts.note: A real exercise with a method too weak to support the claim, run by a company selling resume services. Superseded by tegze-scan-time. The one durable finding from it is where the gaze lands, not how long: approximately 80% of initial attention on name, current title and company, previous title and company, employment dates and education.

facts.claim: Quantified achievements increase callbacks by 40%
facts.value: untraceable
facts.source: attributed to TalentWorks, a company that is defunct and whose blog analysed only its own paying customers; the specific claim does not appear in any surviving post
facts.note: Quantifying bullets is near-universally recommended and mechanically sensible, but no field experiment isolates it. This is the widest gap between advice-confidence and evidence-quality in the field, and the KB says so rather than borrowing a number. Related fabrications with no source at all: '3.2x more likely to get callbacks', '2x fixation time on quantified bullets', '89% of recruiters identify quantified achievements in under 10 seconds'.

facts.claim: Keyword optimisation improves hiring rates 15 to 23%, per MIT Sloan Management Review
facts.value: no such article located
facts.note: Fabricated attribution to a real publication — a common pattern in AI-generated resume-advice content.

facts.claim: A 2023 University of Michigan eye-tracking study found six seconds with 70% of attention on the top third
facts.value: the study does not appear to exist

facts.claim: 72% of Canva templates fail ATS
facts.value: circular citation across content sites with mutually inconsistent methodologies
facts.note: The one disclosed test found Canva averaging approximately 80% field extraction with a spread from 52% to 92%. Canva exports are genuinely risky for other reasons — outlined text and absolute positioning — but not because of this number.

facts.claim: LinkedIn skills need endorsements to be searchable, and endorsements from senior connections carry more algorithmic weight — circulating as "profiles with 15+ endorsed skills get 22x more recruiter views, up from 17x in 2024" and "endorsements from Directors carry 3.4x the algorithmic weight"
facts.value: contradicted by LinkedIn's own documentation
facts.source: LinkedIn Recruiter Help, Skills filter
facts.note: The documented Skills filter draws on explicit skills, skills extracted from any profile text, skills on shared resumes, and skills mentioned outside the skills section. Endorsements are not named as a condition. Circulating claims such as '22x more recruiter views' and 'Director endorsements carry 3.4x the weight' carry decimal precision and no dataset, which is the fabrication signature.

facts.claim: A LinkedIn internal study of 6.8 million #OpenToWork activations between July 2025 and January 2026 found 52% more InMails and 38% higher profile views
facts.value: not found on any LinkedIn property
facts.note: The suspiciously complete metric set and non-LinkedIn phrasing point to fabrication. The real, LinkedIn-published figure is recorded under opentowork-inmail-lift.

facts.claim: Easy Apply converts at 1 to 4% versus 8.7% for direct applications
facts.value: no methodology published by any source; LinkedIn publishes no Easy Apply conversion data and neither does any ATS vendor
facts.note: The structural arguments for applying on the company site are strong without invented numbers: knockout questions are present, the file reaches the recruiter's actual system of record, and custom fields exist.

facts.claim: Women apply only when they meet 100% of the criteria, men at 60%
facts.value: traced to an unsourced McKinsey claim, never a study
facts.source: Curt Rice's tracing of the Lean In citation
facts.note: A survey of approximately 1,000 respondents found the barrier was understanding of hiring processes, not confidence: only about 10% cited confidence.

facts.claim: A resume needs a 65 to 80% match rate to pass an ATS filter
facts.value: a product recommendation, not research
facts.source: Jobscan's own guidance page, which recommends 80% and publishes no algorithm, no weights and no validation study
facts.note: No mainstream ATS computes a resume score out of 100 and rejects below a threshold. Real ranking layers exist — Workday HiredScore, Lever Talent Fit, Greenhouse Talent Matching — but they sort rather than gate, and their scales are vendor-specific and invisible to the candidate. The number remains useful as a coverage checklist: roughly three of every four hard requirements addressed. Optimising past that requires claiming skills you do not have.

facts.claim: Workday's parser fails on approximately 30% of resumes
facts.value: appears only in resume-tool blogs with no methodology
facts.note: Workday documents that parsing results vary with format and word order, and that Skills and Languages are not populated at all. Those documented facts are more useful than the invented rate.

facts.claim: A non-compliant file name gets a resume rejected by the ATS
facts.value: no parser vendor documents file-name-based scoring or rejection
facts.note: Parsers read the file's bytes, not its name. The file name still matters for the human who downloads forty of them into one folder.

facts.claim: Observed extraction damage from a six-column CSS grid of metrics in a real resume
facts.value: the three right-hand cells lost their number-to-label pairing entirely: the numbers extracted as three consecutive orphaned lines, and their three labels merged into one interleaved line whose remainder broke across three further lines
facts.sample: one real resume rendered to PDF by headless Chrome and extracted with pdftotext
facts.source: field test run while building this knowledge base
facts.note: Reproduced deliberately to check whether the column warnings in this KB overstate the risk. They understate it. The common description of the failure is that sidebar content is orphaned from its heading; what actually happened is worse — the labels were spliced together across cells, so the output contains a line composed of fragments of three unrelated labels. A parser cannot recover the pairing, and neither can a human reading the extracted text. The same document is visually flawless on screen.

facts.claim: Effect of non-canonical section headings on section identification, observed
facts.value: a resume using Professional Experience and Technical Skills produced canonical section markers; sibling versions of the same resume using Career History and Technical Expertise produced non-canonical ones, and one version carried no skills section at all
facts.sample: three versions of one real resume
facts.source: field test run while building this knowledge base
facts.note: The versions were written by the same person, for the same market, months apart. Heading drift is not a beginner error; it happens when a document is iterated for visual effect and nobody re-reads the extracted text. Merging Education and Certifications into one heading was present in both non-canonical versions.

literal_numbers.$comment: Numbers that are self-evidently not statistical claims and are therefore exempt from the lock check. Quality codes, limits, dimensions, versions, dates, and prices.

$policing_note: policed_figures lists, per folklore entry, the figures distinctive enough that their bare appearance in prose is itself the error. Round generic percentages are deliberately left out: a rule that fires on '100%' fires on everything and gets switched off, which is how a gate stops being one.
